title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Incident Reviews, Operational Tooling, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This page defines Redwood Inference SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning and forecasting, reliability initiatives and OKRs, incident review standards, operational tooling, and canonical SRE runbooks. The intent is to provide a single, operationally actionable reference for service owners and on-call SREs.

Use this document to:
- Establish consistent SLO definitions and error budget policies across model-serving and control-plane services.
- Align capacity planning practices across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Standardize incident reviews, RCA expectations, and follow-up work.
- Provide repeatable runbooks for common operational events.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets: definitions and examples

Principles
- SLOs are user-facing metrics that reflect reliability expectations for a customer journey (e.g., request success, latency for API surface).
- SLOs must be measurable, owned, and have an incident-response policy (error budget actions) attached.
- Keep SLOs small in number per service (3 max): one availability/ correctness metric, one latency metric, and optionally one resource/throughput metric.

Required metadata for every SLO
- SLO name (short)
- Service / route (e.g., api.redwood.com /v1/generate)
- Metric and PromQL or query used to compute the SLI
- SLO target (percent) and measurement window (rolling 30d default)
- Error budget (100% - SLO) and burn policy thresholds
- Owner(s) and escalation contact

Example SLO table (text table)
| SLO name | Service / route | SLI definition (PromQL) | Target | Window | Owner |
|---------|-----------------|-------------------------|--------|--------|-------|
| Generation success rate | api.hosted/v1/generate | sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api",route="/v1/generate",status!~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api",route="/v1/generate"}[5m])) | 99.9% | 30d | runtime-sre@redwood.com |
| P99 latency (inference token) | api.hosted/v1/generate | histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="api",route="/v1/generate"}[5m])) by (le)) | < 200ms | 30d | runtime-sre@redwood.com |
| Embedding throughput (per-GPU) | serving.gpu-pool | avg(rate(embedding_requests_total[5m])) per GPU | >= 100 qps | 30d | infra-capacity@redwood.com |

Error budget policy (recommended standard)
- Measurement window: rolling 30 days (default).
- Burn thresholds and actions (applied per service):
  - Green: 0-20% budget used 
    normal operations.
  - Yellow: 20-50% budget used 
    notify owner, run reliability checklist, postpone non-critical deploys.
  - Red: 50-100% budget used 
    freeze feature rollouts, prioritize remediation CRs, schedule war room if burn rate > 1%/24h.
  - Critical: 100%+ budget used 
    immediate mitigation required, possible SLA notifications to customers.

Error budget runbook summary
1. Alerting: When a burn threshold is crossed, an automated PagerDuty incident is created with tag error-budget and burn-rate details.
2. Triage: Owner acknowledges within 30 minutes; SRE lead performs quick impact assessment (30 minutes).
3. Mitigation: If in Red/Critical, pause deploy pipeline for the service and open a dedicated incident channel (Slack/Zoom).
4. Follow-up: Create an action plan within 48 hours and include at least one durability/throughput improvement or rollback.

2) Capacity planning and forecasting

Scope and cadence
- Apply to: hosted API tier, dedicated GPU pools, private deployment sizing guidance.
- Cadence: weekly short-term (7-14 days), monthly forecast (30-90 days), quarterly capacity review (90 days+).

Forecasting inputs
- Historical qps and token rates (by route and model family).
- Growth signals: new customers, active experiments, marketing campaigns, enterprise contract starts.
- Model mix and quantization profile (e.g., Llama2-70B fp16 vs quantized-int8 throughput).
- Scheduled maintenance and known change windows.

Planning rules of thumb
- Headroom: maintain 20-30% usable headroom for hosted pools during normal operations; increase to 40% for major product launches.
- Autoscaling config: prefer short warm-up autoscale policies for stateless control-plane services; for stateful/long-lived inference kernels, prefer conservative scale steps with pre-warming pools.
- Reserved capacity: Dedicated customers must commit to a baseline (monthly) and specify burst policy. Runbook includes exact sizing template (see below).

Capacity sizing template (text table)
| Component | Metric | Measurement | Headroom | Owner |
|-----------|--------|-------------|----------|-------|
| GPU pool (g4dn-type) | baseline qps | 95th percentile qps (30d) | 25% headroom | infra-capacity@redwood.com |
| Streaming API | concurrent connections | peak concurrent (7d) | 30% headroom | runtime-sre@redwood.com |

Operational steps for spikes
1. Short-term spike (minutes-hours): enable additional burst capacity if configured, increase worker replicas, and temporarily raise request concurrency limits.
2. Sustained increased demand (days): schedule capacity procurement (cloud GPU request), re-balance model placement, and engage sales/CS for customer communication.

3) Reliability initiatives and metrics (OKRs)

Quarterly objectives (examples)
- O1: Reduce P99 tail latency for /v1/generate by 25% across hosted tier.
- O2: Decrease incidents causing customer-visible errors by 40% quarter-over-quarter.
- O3: Increase automated mitigation coverage (runbooks and auto-remediation) to 80% for top-10 alert classes.

Programs and owners
- Kernel and scheduler optimizations (eng-serving-runtime) 
  lead: Maya Singh.
- Autoscaling and pre-warming enhancements (eng-infra) 
  lead: Daniel Park.
- Observability coverage (eng-platform) 
  lead: Priya Nair.

Success metrics
- MTTR (median) target: < 30 minutes for P1 incidents.
- Change failure rate (rollout-induced incidents): < 1% per major release.
- Automated remediation coverage: percent of alerts with a verified auto-action > 80%.

4) Incident review and postmortem standards

When to run a postmortem
- Any P1 or high-impact P2 incident affecting customers or causing significant capacity/financial impact.
- Any incident where SLOs or error budget policies were materially impacted.

Postmortem template (required fields)
- Title and incident ID
- Date/time (start, detection, mitigation, resolution)
- Impact summary (customers affected, SLOs impacted, cost)
- Timeline (ordered, with timestamps)
- Root cause analysis (multiple hypotheses evaluated and evidence for final RCA)
- Contributing factors (process, tooling, capacity, code)
- Remediation actions (owner, ETA, verification criteria)
- Lessons learned and follow-up tickets (link to JIRA)
- Blamelessness statement and review sign-off (service owner, SRE lead)

Postmortem process
1. Draft: initial draft within 72 hours of incident resolution.
2. Review: reviewers (owner, SRE lead, infra lead) must comment within 7 days.
3. Publish: final postmortem published in Confluence within 14 days with action items tracked to completion.

5) Operational tooling and observability standards

Monitoring stack (standard)
- Metrics: Prometheus for core metrics, recorded rules for SLI calculation.
- Tracing: Honeycomb for distributed traces and tail latency analysis.
- Dashboards: Grafana with per-service SLO dashboard templates (latency, success rate, capacity).
- Logging: structured logs to Loki/Cloud logging with request_id and model_id fields.
- Error tracking: Sentry for control-plane exceptions.
- Alerting: PagerDuty for paging on-call; alerts defined in Alertmanager with runbook links.

Dashboard and alert hygiene
- Every production service must have: SLO dashboard, capacity dashboard, top-10 traces dashboard, and an alert-to-runbook mapping.
- Alert definitions must include: symptom, severity (P1/P2/P3), SRE owner, and exact runbook link.
- Rate-limit noisy alerts with aggregation windows and suppression rules; use dedup keys for similar events.

Operational tooling examples
- SLO burn dashboard: Grafana panel showing rolling 30d burn, daily burn-rate, and predicted exhaustion date.
- On-call tools: PagerDuty rotation, Slack channel #oncall-runtime, and bridging playbooks for Zoom immediate response.

6) Canonical SRE runbooks (examples)

Runbook: High tail latency for /v1/generate (P99 elevated)
- Symptoms (how alerted): p99_latency > 200ms for 15m, SLO burn enters Yellow/Red.
- Immediate actions (first 15 minutes):
  1. Acknowledge PagerDuty incident and open incident channel.
  2. Check Grafana SLO & capacity dashboards and Honeycomb traces to determine whether tail is model-level or infra-level.
  3. If traces show kernel stalls or OOM: check GPU memory usage (prometheus query: avg_over_time(nvidia_gpu_memory_used_bytes[5m]) by (instance)).
  4. If model-level (single model causing tail): route traffic to a lower-latency model variant (traffic-split API) and scale up pool for that model.
  5. If infra-level (node saturating): cordon node, shift traffic, and spin up pre-warmed node/pool.
- Commands and checks:
  - kubectl get pods -n runtime -l service=runtime -o wide
  - promql: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="api"}[5m])) by (le))
  - gpu check: ssh gpu-host && nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,utilization.gpu --format=csv
- Escalation: After 30 minutes if no mitigation, escalate to SRE lead and Eng runtime (pagerduty escalation).
- Post-incident: run capacity/placement analysis and add a mitigation (auto-route to fallback) if not already present.

Runbook: Model OOM during inference
- Symptoms: OOM errors surfaced in logs, model process restart loops, increased 5xx rate for requests to specific model.
- Immediate actions:
  1. Acknowledge and isolate the node (mark unschedulable).
  2. Remove the model from autoscaler rotation for the pool.
  3. If a recent model change or quantization profile was rolled out, rollback to previous artifact.
  4. Check model size and memory settings. If memory exceeds expected, increase GPU memory reservation or switch to a larger-instance pool.
- Commands:
  - kubectl logs <pod> -n runtime --tail=200
  - kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
  - check model artifact: gsutil ls gs://models/release/<model>/
- Follow-up: Update model onboarding checklist to include memory profile for 1,2,5,10 token sequences and add automated preflight tests.

Runbook ownership and maintenance
- Each runbook must include: owner (person/team), last verified date, and verification steps.
- Runbook review cadence: quarterly for critical runbooks, annually for lower-priority ones.

Appendix A: Example alert-to-runbook mapping (text table)
| Alert name | Symptom | Severity | Runbook link | Owner |
|------------|---------|----------|-------------|-------|
| P99 latency spike - /v1/generate | p99 > 200ms | P1/P2 | /confluence/eng-sre/sre-runbook-high-tail-latency | runtime-sre@redwood.com |
| Model OOM | process restarts, 5xx | P1 | /confluence/eng-sre/sre-runbook-model-oom | eng-serving-runtime@redwood.com |
| Error budget burn > 50% | projected exhaustion < 7 days | P2 | /confluence/eng-sre/sre-error-budget-runbook | runtime-sre@redwood.com |

Appendix B: SLO calculation examples (PromQL)
- Success rate SLI (30m):
  sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api",route="/v1/generate",status!~"5.."}[30m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api",route="/v1/generate"}[30m]))
- P99 latency (5m rolling):
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="api"}[5m])) by (le))

Appendix C: Contact and escalation list
- Runtime SRE on-call: pagerduty rotation "runtime-sre" (page sequence applied).
- Infra capacity: infra-capacity@redwood.com.
- Incident comms: incident-comms@redwood.com.

Governance and change process
- Any change to SLO targets or runbook critical steps must be reviewed by SRE lead and product owner and published with a changelog entry in Confluence.
- Quarterly SLO review meeting required for all services with published SLOs to validate targets, measurement queries, and owner responsibilities.

End of document.
